earlier_research.fact: Where the scramble leaves the trail
earlier_research.correct_value: The climbers' path leaves at an unsigned fork/broad saddle about half a mile on the Hurricane Ridge side of the Switchback Trail junction (about 2.5 mi from the visitor center); Victor Pass is up the other branch and is not the summit route.
earlier_research.evidence: The Mount Angeles hike page puts the climbers' trail fork about 2.5 mi from Hurricane Ridge, branching left; its Klahhane Ridge page puts the Switchback junction 3.1 mi from Hurricane Ridge and Victor Pass a further climb beyond it. Another guide says to go west about half a mile from the Switchback junction to a spur heading north to the summit, and a route page describes turning south from the Switchback junction about 0.5 mi to a broad saddle where the climbers' trail leaves. None put the departure at Victor Pass.

earlier_research.correct_value: Switchback Trail: ~700 ft in 0.6 mi to the junction with the trail from Hurricane Ridge (the summit route turns off here); ~1,500 ft in 1.5 mi only if continuing to Victor Pass.
earlier_research.evidence: Both figures are real but for different segments: 700 ft in 0.6 mi to the Mount Angeles trail junction, and 1,500 ft in 1.5 mi to Victor Pass. The beta used the Victor Pass figure for the summit route; the beta rewrite (see the fork fix) now uses the 0.6-mi figure, matching the approach. The bivy note's 'close to 1,000 ft in under a mile' is in bivy[], which is owned by the camping clean-up and is not patched here.

earlier_research.correct_value: Class 3
earlier_research.evidence: The hike page calls the final push a class 3 scramble; another guide says to plan on Class 3 at a minimum; a route page and a trip report describe class 2 ledges with class 3 steps at the top. No source gives Class 4.

The row itself is split three fields (descent_text, climbing_route[2], approach) against three (itinerary note, schedule 'Reverse the route', descent). ice axe (recommended if snow lingers, typically before mid-July)

row.overview: Mount Angeles (6,454 ft) is the highest point between Hurricane Ridge and the Strait of Juan de Fuca, rising as a prominent, accessible summit above the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center in the northern Olympics. It's reached by trail almost the whole way, with a short, loose Class 3 scramble guarding the true summit. On a clear day the top gives views across the Strait of Juan de Fuca to Vancouver Island, north to the San Juans, south into the interior Olympics toward Mount Olympus, and (in good visibility) east to Mount Rainier.
row.beta: From the Switchback Trailhead on Hurricane Ridge Road, hike the Switchback Trail steeply up through subalpine forest (about 700 ft in 0.6 mile) to its junction with the trail from Hurricane Ridge. Turn left and follow that trail roughly half a mile to a broad saddle, where an unsigned climbers' path forks off uphill toward the summit; the maintained trail that climbs on to Victor Pass (5,850 ft) is not the summit route. Take the climbers' path and scramble Class 3 terrain over loose rock/talus to the summit. There is no roped climbing on the standard route, but the exposure and loose rock warrant caution and route-finding care.
row.turnaround: Most parties budget roughly 4-6 hours car-to-car from the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center; set a firm early-afternoon turnaround time to be off the exposed ridge and summit block before typical late-summer thunderstorm build-up.
row.permit: Olympic National Park: no permit for day climbs; all overnight wilderness stays require a wilderness camping permit via Recreation.gov.
row.descent: Reverse the route: downclimb the loose Class 3 summit block carefully and facing in, regain the climbers trail through the scree bowl, and follow it back down to the Klahhane Ridge Trail junction, then the High Ridge/Sunrise Ridge Trail to the Visitor Center (or down the Switchback Trail if you looped up via Klahhane Ridge). The downclimb is often slower and more consequential than the ascent — watch for rockfall dislodged by your own party funneling onto anyone below, and budget extra time.

waypoints.name: Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center (High Ridge Trailhead)
waypoints.note: Start at the east end of the Hurricane Ridge parking lot on the paved Cirque Rim path onto High Ridge Trail; restrooms/potable water here in summer, none beyond this point.
waypoints.directions: Drive Hurricane Ridge Road about 17 miles south from Port Angeles — Race Street off Highway 101 — to the road's end at the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center, around 5,250 ft. Park in the visitor center lot and start at its east end, on the paved Cirque Rim path onto the High Ridge Trail. Come early, since parking here fills. The seasonal contact station has restrooms and potable water, and it is the last of either — there is no reliable water anywhere past the lot.

waypoints.note: Optional 0.2-mi dead-end spur to a panoramic overlook; stay on the main High Ridge/Sunrise Ridge Nature Trail toward Klahhane Ridge to continue.

waypoints.name: Morse Creek valley overlook spur
waypoints.note: Short spur trail to a viewpoint over the Morse Creek/Elwha drainages; roughly 800 ft of the day's climbing is behind you and the trail steepens above.

waypoints.name: Mount Angeles trail fork (Klahhane Ridge split)

row.pro_needs: No technical rock pro on the standard line; the crux is a short exposed Class 3 scramble.
row.best_season: Late July through September is most reliable for a dry, snow-free scramble; in heavy-snow years lingering, rotten snow patches on the approach and in the summit gully can persist into July or even August. Early-season parties (June–early July) should be prepared for glissade-able but potentially rotten snow and consider carrying an ice axe. The route is generally out of condition (and Hurricane Ridge Road itself has very limited access) from roughly mid-December through March.
row.approach: From the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center parking lot (end of Hurricane Ridge Road, ~17 mi south of Port Angeles via Race St/Hwy 101), start on the paved High Ridge Trail at the east end of the lot. At about 0.3 mi bear toward Sunrise Point/Klahhane Ridge Trail and continue along open, exposed subalpine ridge (alternating meadow and pocket forest) for roughly 2.5 mi to an unsigned junction where a distinct, unmaintained 'climbers trail' splits left (west) off the maintained Klahhane Ridge Trail — this is the start of the true scramble route (sometimes mapped as the Mount Angeles Summit Climbers Trail). A shorter, steeper alternative start exists directly off Hurricane Ridge Road at the Switchback Trail (~mile marker in the last few miles before the visitor center), which gains about 700-800 ft in 0.6 mi to meet the Mount Angeles Trail higher up, cutting off some of the ridge walk. From the climbers-trail junction, the primitive use trail climbs steeply through rocky meadows and thinning forest on the peak's west side — this final push is only about 0.6 mi but does roughly 800 of the route's 2,100 total feet of gain (average grade ~27%, max ~42%), topping out around 6,000 ft at the base of the summit block/gully. Route-finding note from on-the-ground reports: don't scramble the first notch you reach — stay on the faint boot path traversing higher to the actual summit gully. From there, most parties scramble the right/east side of the final block, which is loose, fractured 'rotten' rock (the same line the descent explicitly avoids downclimbing) with only brief but exposed final moves to the true summit (6,454 ft). There is no reliable water past the visitor center (which has a seasonal contact station with restrooms/potable water) — carry all you need. Key hazards: lingering rotten/consolidated snow choking the summit notch/gully well into July and August even in normal years, loose scree and fractured, rockfall-prone rock on the upper scramble, and sustained exposure along the open ridge crest.
row.descent_text: Descend the same way you came up as far as the base of the summit block, but do NOT reverse the ascent gully — parties consistently and strongly recommend downclimbing the left (west) side of the summit block/notch instead, since the direct/right-side ascent line is loose, fractured 'rotten' rock that can trigger rockfall or a slide if downclimbed. This is a class 3 scramble downclimb only; there are no fixed anchors, bolts, or rappel stations reported anywhere on the standard route, and roped rappelling is not reported as part of the normal descent — a rope is not standard gear here, though a cautious party could choose to hand-line or belay the notch with a single rope and natural gear (a tree/horn sling) if conditions (verglas, wet rock, inexperienced members) warrant it. Below the block, pick back up the primitive climbers trail, drop back to the Klahhane Ridge Trail junction, and retrace the ridge trail (or the Switchback Trail cutoff, if that was your approach) back to the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center — roughly 3.1 mi and 1.5-2 hours from the summit for the average party. Stay alert on the descent specifically at the loose scree below the block and on the exposed notch downclimb: parties often flag descent, not ascent, as the more dangerous part of this route because of accumulated fatigue plus loose rock underfoot.
row.bail: Retreat is straightforward on the approach trail right up until the final summit block; once committed to the exposed Class 3 rock, downclimbing the way you came is generally the only realistic option, so don't push a large group or inexperienced scramblers onto the block in marginal conditions.

itinerary.cal: Snow can linger on the upper scree/scramble sections into July or August; check recent trip reports before a spring/early-summer attempt.

days.note: Start early from the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center on the paved High Ridge Trail, join the Klahhane Ridge Trail, then peel off onto the climbers' trail through meadows and a scree bowl to the base of the summit block. A short, exposed Class 3 scramble on loose rock gains the true (south) summit; reverse the same line to descend. Whole outing is a straightforward day hike/scramble with no camping involved.

access.fees: NPS entrance fee required: $30/private vehicle (7-day pass), $25/motorcycle, $15/person on foot or bike; Olympic-specific annual pass $55; America the Beautiful passes accepted. Park does not accept cash — card/electronic payment only.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Standard Leave No Trace / NPS wilderness rules apply beyond the trailhead: no dogs or bikes on trail, stay on the established boot path on the summit block to limit erosion, pack out all trash.
access.permit: No permit needed for a day scramble. A wilderness permit (via recreation.gov, $8/person/night + $6 non-refundable reservation fee, or covered by the $45 Annual Wilderness Pass) is only required if camping overnight in the backcountry.
access.closures: Hurricane Ridge Road is gated nightly and, in winter (roughly mid-Dec–late March), is plowed and open for uphill travel only Friday–Sunday (plus a few holiday exceptions) from about 9am–4pm; traction tires/chains are often required. The Hurricane Ridge Day Lodge burned down in an unexplained May 2023 fire and has not been rebuilt: the park's reconstruction page (updated August 25, 2026) lists the project in design, with construction starting in 2028 at the earliest, so there are no indoor visitor facilities at the top — only temporary restroom trailers, and no water or food. The road has also had periodic multi-day closures for rockfall/unstable slopes, and summer 2026 utility work and meadow-trail construction may cause intermittent weekday impacts. Check the NPS current road conditions page or call (360) 565-3131 before driving up.
access.landManager: Olympic National Park — the Hurricane Ridge day-use corridor is developed, non-wilderness NPS land; the route crosses into the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness along Klahhane Ridge beyond the immediate visitor-center area
access.land_manager: National Park Service — Olympic National Park (Olympic Wilderness)

road.name: Hurricane Ridge Road
road.status: Paved; generally open daily May–October weather permitting. In winter (~mid-Dec–late March) it's plowed and open for uphill travel only Fri–Sun (plus select holidays), 9am–4pm, with chains/traction tires commonly required.
road.driveNote: From Hwy 101 in Port Angeles (~milepost 249): south on Race St 1.2 mi, then right/south onto Hurricane Ridge Road; continue 17.5 mi to the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center lot, or 14.8 mi to the Switchback Trailhead pullout for the shorter, steeper start.
road.seasonalGate: Heart O' the Hills entrance station gate, closed nightly outside posted hours and closed on non-plow days in winter.

climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate with strong orographic effect — the Hurricane Ridge area receives on the order of 85+ inches of precipitation per year, much of it as heavy winter snowpack, with drier, more stable weather typical in July–September. Cloud and fog off the Strait can sock in the ridge even on otherwise clear days.

bySeason.fall: Shortening days and the first snow can arrive by October; road access and trail conditions become more variable.
bySeason.spring: Heavy lingering snowpack on approach slopes and in the summit gully well into June in many years; not a realistic scramble window without snow travel experience and gear.
bySeason.summer: Jul–Sep is the primary climbing season; typically the most stable weather but afternoon thunderstorms and fast-moving marine cloud can still develop.
bySeason.winter: Essentially inaccessible for this route — Hurricane Ridge Road is only plowed/open Friday–Sunday (plus limited holidays) and the peak becomes a full winter mountaineering objective.

emergency.notes: Cell coverage is unreliable to nonexistent on the ridge and summit block; the most reliable signal is generally back at the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center parking lot. Carry a way to signal for help (whistle, satellite communicator) if scrambling with a small party.
emergency.rangerStation: Olympic National Park Wilderness Information Center, 3002 Mount Angeles Rd, Port Angeles, WA 98362 — (360) 565-3100
emergency.nearestHospital: Olympic Medical Center, 939 Caroline St, Port Angeles, WA — roughly 20 miles / 35-40 minutes drive from the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911 (routed to Clallam County Sheriff/Olympic NP dispatch for SAR)

crowds.peakTraffic: Weekends July-August, especially midday, when Hurricane Ridge Road/visitor area is busiest; the Klahhane Ridge approach trail sees the most foot traffic (day hikers, not all continuing to the scramble)
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Very popular; likely on the order of dozens of parties per summer weekend near Hurricane Ridge, tapering to a handful on weekdays and on the actual Class 3 summit block

fitnessSpec.hiking: Solid day-hike fitness for several miles of trail plus a steep off-trail climb through meadows/subalpine forest to reach the scramble
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light day pack (roughly 10-15 lb: water, layers, helmet, snacks)

approach_variants.notes: Paved path off the east end of the visitor centre lot, then open subalpine ridge for about two and a half miles to an unsigned split. A shorter, steeper start climbs from the Switchback Trail on the road below and joins higher up. Nothing dependable to drink past the visitor centre — carry it all.

Rockfall funnelling down the crux gully onto anyone below

Fast-building afternoon storms on a fully exposed ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding: The climbers' path leaves the maintained Klahhane Ridge Trail at an unsigned fork roughly 2.3 miles out: bear left and uphill to the west, where the maintained tread carries on right along the ridge toward Victor Pass and Lake Angeles. From the fork the primitive path climbs rocky meadow on the peak's west side and does about eight hundred of the day's feet in a little over half a mile, topping out near 6,000 ft in a scree bowl beneath the summit block. The identification that matters here is which notch, and it catches people every season: do not scramble the first notch you reach. The boot path keeps traversing higher and the gully that goes is further along, directly beneath the true summit. Stay on the worn tread climber's-left of the open scree fan rather than going straight up the fan itself, which is the rockfall funnel. You are at the base when the meadow ends and you are standing on dirty, fractured ledges with a roughly forty-foot exposed step above you. If the ground has levelled off or you are back on maintained tread heading toward Lake Angeles, you have overshot.

climbing_route.label: Climbers' trail up the west side
climbing_route.notes: At the unsigned junction roughly 2.5 mi along the Klahhane Ridge Trail, a distinct unmaintained climbers' trail splits left (west) — the start of the true scramble. The primitive use trail climbs steeply through rocky meadows and thinning forest on the peak's west side: only about 0.6 mi but roughly 800 of the route's 2,100 ft of gain (average grade ~27%, max ~42%), topping out around 6,000 ft at the base of the summit block/gully. Sustained exposure along the open ridge crest below.

climbing_route.label: Traverse to the summit gully
climbing_route.notes: Do not scramble the first notch you reach — stay on the faint boot path traversing higher to the actual summit gully. Rotten, consolidated snow can choke the summit notch/gully well into July and August even in normal years.

climbing_route.label: Final summit block
climbing_route.notes: Most parties scramble the right/east side of the final block on loose, fractured 'rotten' rock — the same line the descent explicitly avoids downclimbing. Brief but exposed final moves to the true summit at 6,454 ft. Loose scree and rockfall-prone rock throughout the upper scramble.

bivy.name: Heart o' the Hills campground
bivy.notes: This is the staging base for Mount Angeles and it is a staging base only — it is a few miles up the Hurricane Ridge road from Port Angeles, and no part of the climb passes through it. The scramble itself starts from a pull-out around mile 15 on that road, where the Switchback trail gains close to 1,000 ft in under a mile to Klahhane Ridge, then a short westward stretch and a spur onto the unmaintained final ridge — exposed walking and class 3 on loose fractured rock to the 6,454 ft summit. It is a day trip for a fit party, so this camp exists for the group that starts late, gets weathered off, or wants to be at the trailhead at first light. Read the road before you count on it: in winter the Hurricane Ridge road is plowed and open only Friday through Sunday plus a few holiday dates, with uphill traffic released from mid-morning, and it closes without notice in bad weather. Recent seasons have also brought midweek closures for utility work in the weeks after Memorial Day, so check the current schedule rather than assuming summer means open. Because there are no reservations, arrive early on a summer weekend.
bivy.water: Drinking water on tap, flush toilets and rubbish collection through the season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — frontcountry campground, nightly fee paid on site, park entrance fee applies. Fires permitted in the provided rings unless a seasonal ban is in force, which happens most late summers on this peninsula.
bivy.capacity: Around 105 single-family sites in old growth, taking tents and rigs up to about 24 ft with a few longer; first-come, first-served with no reservations

name: Standard Scramble (Marmot Lake / O'Neil Pass approach)
prior_findings: Marmot Lake camp card says 1.1 mi above Upper Duckabush; trail is ~3.5 mi. The area record's elevation_ft 6,232 should be 6,254. The approach still names sources ('per NPS', 'in the regional climbers guide').

earlier_research.correct_value: The standard lines go up the south side (South Ridge or Middle Peak's south side) from O'Neil Pass; the north side holds glaciers/permanent snowfields.
earlier_research.evidence: The Olympic Mountain Rescue climbers' guide lists only two routes, both Grade I Class 4 'via O'Neil Pass and Middle Peak' and 'via O'Neil Pass and the South Ridge', and notes north-side glaciers/year-round snowfields. row.name: Standard Scramble (Marmot Lake / O'Neil Pass approach)
hazards: Loose rock and short exposed steps near the multiple summits
Steep snow on the upper slopes into early summer, with possible cornices on north/east-facing sections of the summit ridge in spring conditions
Several closely spaced summits: the main summit (6,254 ft) is the high point, with the slightly lower East Peak (about 6,233 ft) roughly 0.3 mi away, so confirm which top you are on

row.overview: Mount Duckabush (6,254 ft) is a remote, multi-summit peak in the Skokomish–LaCrosse group of the central Olympic Mountains, within Olympic National Park's Daniel J. Evans Wilderness, on the divide between the Duckabush River headwaters and La Crosse Basin near Marmot Lake and O'Neil Pass. A subsidiary East Peak (about 6,233 ft), roughly 0.3 miles from the main summit, is slightly lower, and some parties tag both. With only a handful of logged ascents on record, it's one of the least-visited named summits in the range, owing to an approach that runs 20+ trail miles one-way before any off-trail scrambling even starts.
row.beta: Mount Duckabush has almost no published route-by-route beta online. It is climbed as a remote scramble objective from the Marmot Lake basin or O'Neil Pass area reached via the Duckabush River Trail, in the same general high country used to reach neighboring Mount Steel (whose standard routes, via First Divide and via the Marmot Lake Trail, are both rated Class 1). Duckabush itself is steeper and less documented than Steel; treat any specific class rating as unconfirmed - the definitive description for this peak was not available.
row.turnaround: Given the multi-day approach and remote, unmaintained nature of the terrain, set a firm turnaround time that leaves ample daylight margin to regain the trail at Marmot Lake before dark, with extra buffer for stream crossings and route-finding on the return.
row.comms: Deep wilderness valley and alpine terrain in Olympic National Park; cell coverage is generally unreliable to absent along the Duckabush River valley and in the Marmot Lake/O'Neil Pass high country. Carry a satellite messenger/PLB for this approach.
row.descent: Reverse the approach: descend the off-trail talus/heather (and any snow) back to O'Neil Pass or Marmot Lake, then retrace the Duckabush River Trail roughly 20 miles to the trailhead — most parties split this over one or two more camp nights rather than doing it in a single push.

row.pro_needs: No technical rock pro on the standard line; an ice axe helps on early-season snow slopes.
row.best_season: Mid-July through September — earlier trips still often face lingering snow on Big Hump, around Marmot Lake, and on the final summit slopes.
row.approach: From the Duckabush Trailhead (end of Forest Service Road 2510, ~440 ft, reached via US-101 south of Quilcene), follow the Duckabush River Trail #803 upriver. The first ~2.4 miles run at an easy grade along the river through old-growth forest, then the trail climbs steadily and at times steeply (~1,000 ft) to crest Big Hump at about mile 3.9 — the trail's first real obstacle, made looser and more exposed to sun/blowdown by a 2011 human-caused fire that scorched a swath of old growth on the Hump. Past Big Hump the trail drops back toward the river and continues upvalley through Five-Mile and Ten-Mile Camps, with several unbridged side-creek crossings that are normally an easy rock-hop but can be a real ford during spring snowmelt or after heavy rain. Beyond Upper Duckabush Camp the trail leaves the valley floor and switchbacks up out of the drainage, gaining roughly 2,000 ft over the final ~3 miles through forest to reach Marmot Lake (~4,400 ft), a reliable-water high camp at roughly 19-20 trail miles from the trailhead (the Duckabush/O'Neil Pass corridor runs 16+ miles from the park boundary alone, per NPS). From Marmot Lake it's a little over a mile more, skirting a ridge with Quinault-valley views, to O'Neil Pass (~4,950 ft). This is a serious multi-day backpack approach with no realistic car-to-summit day-trip option; nearly all parties camp at Marmot Lake or O'Neil Pass and climb the peak from there. From at or near O'Neil Pass, leave the maintained trail and head cross-country (no path, talus and heather benches) toward Duckabush's south side to reach either the base of the South Ridge or the south aspect of Middle Peak — both listed as Grade I, Class 4 lines in the regional climbers' guide. Snow and small permanent snowfields persist on the mountain's north side well into summer, so the south-side/ridge lines are the standard route; carry an ice axe for lingering snow on the benches and approach slopes in early season (snow commonly lingers on the high trail and upper slopes into July). An alternate approach reaches the same high camp via the Dosewallips River Trail and Anderson Pass area rather than the Duckabush River Trail.
row.descent_text: There is no separate descent line — parties down-climb the same Class 3-4 talus and rock terrain (South Ridge or Middle Peak's south side, per whichever line was climbed) back down to the cross-country benches below, then pick up the O'Neil Pass Trail again near the pass and retrace the Duckabush River Trail back over Big Hump to the trailhead. No fixed or bolted rappel anchors are documented anywhere on this peak, and the route is graded Grade I (a route completable, up and down, in a single push from camp), which by Olympic grading convention implies no planned rope work beyond scrambling protection. That said, Class 4 terrain carries real exposure and loose rock, so a competent party should still carry a light rope, a few slings, and some nuts as a contingency to belay or hand-line an exposed step near the summit block, especially if wet rock, verglas, or overhanging north-side snow patches are encountered — but this would be an improvised single-pitch lower, not a planned multi-rappel descent.
row.bail: Retreat is simply reversing the trail, but it's long — from O'Neil Pass/Marmot Lake it's still ~20 miles back to the trailhead, so set a camp-to-camp turnaround time rather than planning to bail all the way to the car in one push.

itinerary.cal: The Duckabush River Trail is open: the park's Bear Gulch Fire closures are on the Staircase side (the North Fork Skokomish, Home Sweet Home and Six Ridge trails), with no reopening date on the park's trail-conditions page updated September 14, 2026, and no Forest Service alert lists the Duckabush road or trail. The same page reports more than 50 downed trees between the trailhead and the Upper Duckabush ford — check it before planning this trip.

climate.summer: Generally the clearest and most stable window, favored for the long approach and any high-country travel.
climate.winter: Heavy precipitation and snow at elevation typical of Olympic winters; the Duckabush watershed drains high, glaciated terrain that gets deep snowpack.
climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate typical of the interior Olympics: wet, mild winters with heavy snowfall at this elevation, and drier, clearer summers as Pacific high pressure builds — but orographic lift means rain and cloud can move in on short notice even in summer.

bySeason.fall: Late-season trips (late Sept–Oct) can find good weather windows but face shorter days and a higher chance of early snow at this elevation.
bySeason.spring: Deep, unstable snowpack typically persists into June–July on north/east aspects and the summit ridge; this is effectively a snow-climb/ski-mountaineering season, not a scramble season.
bySeason.summer: Mid-July–September is the most reliable weather and snow-free window, though afternoon thunderstorms and fast-moving Pacific fronts are still possible.
bySeason.winter: Effectively inaccessible — the Hood Canal side gets heavy rain/snow and the interior Olympics see prolonged storm cycles; no documented winter ascents found.

emergency.notes: One of the most remote standard scrambles in the Olympics — realistically a 3–4 day round trip with no cell coverage. A satellite communicator (inReach/Zoleo) is strongly advised given how long a ground SAR response would take to reach O'Neil Pass/Marmot Lake.

bivy.name: Marmot Lake — the Duckabush-side high camp for Steel and Duckabush
bivy.notes: The eastern base for this group of peaks, about 20 miles up the Duckabush River trail from Brinnon and roughly 1.1 miles and 1,700 ft above the Upper Duckabush camp, in a saddle a little over a mile from O'Neil Pass. Mount Steel and Mount Duckabush both stand directly above it, and Steel's less-travelled route from this side leaves the trail a few miles above the Duckabush camp and follows a small creek into an amphitheatre on the west side of the summit, where easy slopes lead to the top. Mount Duckabush is a scramble from the same basin. THE APPROACH IS THE OBSTACLE, NOT THE CLIMBING. Twenty miles with the Big Hump early on, a river ford in the upper valley that is genuinely hazardous outside high summer, and a trail that goes long stretches between clearings — recent accounts describe dozens of downed trees between the trailhead and the upper ford and heavy brush. Most parties take two full days each way. The compensation is that this side stayed open when the Staircase side was closed by the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire: the park still lists the North Fork Skokomish and Home Sweet Home trails closed, with no reopening date, on the park's trail-conditions page updated September 14, 2026, and while they stay closed this is the direct way in to Steel and Duckabush. Hart and LaCrosse Lakes a mile or two above make excellent extensions if you have the days. Season is mid-July through September.

bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required and must be reserved through the federal recreation booking site. Not one of the named quota camps, but it is remote enough that availability is rarely the problem. Bear canisters are required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at this elevation.

row.overview: Monument Peak is the most rugged and inaccessible peak in the Lago group, deep in the eastern Pasayten Wilderness near the Eureka Creek country. Double-nubbed and built of granite, it sits almost as an island: Eureka Creek wraps its north, west, and south sides while Monument Creek drains the east side. The mountain has a precipitous north/northeast side, a cliffy east face, a rugged west face, and a comparatively gentler (though still remote) south slope that forms the standard scramble line. A disheveled connecting ridge links it to 8,397-ft Blackcap Mountain a half-mile north; 8,745-ft Mount Lago, its line parent, lies about 2.4 miles further north. First ascended in 1978 by Fred Beckey and John Roper.
row.beta: From a high camp near Lake of the Woods or in the Monument-Lake / Lower Monument basin, gain Monument's south ridge crest (~6,900 ft) via a left-angling ramp system, then follow the broad ridge northwest for over a mile on class 2 talus. A false summit near 8,000 ft requires a short, light class 3 scramble; from there one or two more class 3 moves lead to the true 8,597 ft summit, which features a distinctive leaning summit horn. The peak can also be approached from basins on its east/northeast side via the Monument Creek Trail, or from the north via Shellrock Pass.
row.turnaround: This is a long, remote approach (11+ miles one-way with an unmaintained, route-finding-dependent trail beyond Eureka Creek). Set a firm turnaround time based on your actual approach pace and current weather — the final ridge and summit block involve exposed class 3 scrambling that is best done with a comfortable margin to get back to camp before dark or before afternoon thunderstorms build.
row.rock_grade: Class 3 (short class 3/4 moves near the false summit and true summit)
row.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass at some trailheads.
row.descent: Reverse the ascent: down the south-ridge talus to the ramp system and back into Lower Monument Basin. Loose rock makes the talus slower and more hazardous descending than climbing; some parties approaching via the southeast ridge/west basin have down-climbed a Class 3 line on the east face instead, but this is not the standard descent and is not well documented — don't count on it without firsthand beta.

lingering steep snowfield just below the summit into early July
unmaintained, route-finding-dependent approach trail beyond Eureka Creek

waypoints.name: Eureka Creek Ford
waypoints.note: Bridge here washed out in 2006 and was never replaced; ford can be a tricky, thigh-deep crossing in early-season high water, last reliable water before the long dry climb to Pistol Ridge.
waypoints.directions: Follow Monument Creek Trail No. 484 up the Lost River valley. The first 4 miles are well maintained, running through old-growth forest and along rock slopes to the confluence and Eureka Falls Camp. The bridge here washed out in 2006 and was never replaced, so the crossing is a ford; it can run thigh-deep and cold during snowmelt. This is the last easy, reliable water before a long dry climb.

waypoints.name: Pistol Pass
waypoints.note: Abandoned, brushy tread climbs ~4,700 ft from the ford onto Pistol Ridge before improving near the pass; from here the maintained trail effectively ends and route-finding begins.
waypoints.directions: Beyond the ford the trail has been essentially unmaintained for over 25 years, brushy and choked with deadfall, and route-finding becomes real work. Pick up the abandoned tread climbing onto Pistol Ridge and follow it for about 4,700 ft of gain; the tread improves near the top. Expect 4 to 5 hours from the creek and plan on running out of water.

waypoints.name: Lake of the Woods
waypoints.note: Small alpine lake about a mile below Pistol Pass with established campsites; the standard staging camp for the Monument Peak / Lake Mountain 'Monumental Slam.'

waypoints.name: Lake Mountain South Ridge Saddle
waypoints.note: Cross-country gain from Lake of the Woods over Lake Mountain's south ridge saddle, the start of the side-hill traverse toward Monument Peak.
waypoints.directions: Traverse cross-country from the lake, gaining ground over Lake Mountain's south ridge saddle. Reckon on about 2 hours from camp; this is where the side-hill traverse toward Monument Peak begins.

waypoints.name: Lower Monument Basin
waypoints.note: Descend off the saddle into this basin below Monument's south side; used as a bivy/staging spot by parties splitting the peak from Lake Mountain.
waypoints.directions: Drop off the saddle into the basin below Monument's south side, losing about 1,300 ft. The lake-outlet creek here is the last dependable water for the summit push and can be down to a trickle late in the season, so fill up.

waypoints.note: Left-angling ramp system out of Lower Monument Basin gains the crest of the south ridge; this is the ramp used by the descent.
waypoints.directions: From the basin, climb the left-angling ramp system that gains the crest of the south ridge, about 800 ft of ascent. This is the ramp the descent beta also refers to, so note where you topped out.

waypoints.name: Monument Peak Summit
waypoints.note: Long talus traverse along the south ridge ends at the 'leaning summit horn,' with Class 3 scrambling on the final blocks (first ascent Beckey/Roper, 1978).
waypoints.directions: Follow the broad ridge for over a mile of class 2 talus walking toward the summit, with light class 3 in spots. A short class 3 scramble surmounts the false summit near 8,000 ft, then one or two more class 3 moves on the steep upper mountain reach the leaning summit horn. A steep snowfield just below the top sometimes lingers into midsummer and either needs an axe or a class 3-4 rock detour around its left side. Roughly 3 hours from the ridge crest.

row.pro_needs: Unroped class 2-3 scramble; no technical gear normally required.
row.best_season: Late July through September gives the most reliable snow-free travel — trip reports as late as June 30-July 2 encountered summit-area snowfields firm enough to require crampons, and the Harts Pass-area roads/trails typically aren't fully clear of snow until late June or July.
row.approach: Four approaches reach Monument Peak, all long and remote — this is deep in the Pasayten Wilderness near the Canadian border, and most parties treat it as a 2-3 day trip with a high camp. The most common is via the Monument Creek Trailhead on Lost River Road/FR 5400 (about 22 miles northwest of Winthrop via Mazama), starting at roughly 2,400 ft. From the trailhead, follow Monument Creek Trail No. 484 up the Lost River valley; the first ~4 miles are well-maintained through old-growth forest and along rock slopes to the Eureka Creek confluence (Eureka Falls Camp) — this is your last easy, reliable water before a long dry stretch. Beyond Eureka Creek the trail has been essentially unmaintained for 25+ years, brushy and choked with deadfall, and route-finding becomes real work. Ford Eureka Creek (can run thigh-to-waist deep during snowmelt — a genuine early-summer hazard) then pick up the abandoned tread climbing onto Pistol Ridge, following it up to 7,100-ft Pistol Pass around mile 11. From the pass, descend about a mile on the trail, finishing on a short spur, to Lake of the Woods in the Monument–Lake Mountain basin, a common high camp — about 12 miles and 5,300 ft of gain from the trailhead. From camp, traverse cross-country northwest to the ~7,400-ft saddle below Lake Mountain, then descend into Lower Monument Basin (~6,100 ft); the lake-outlet creek here is your last dependable water for the summit push and can shrink to a trickle late in the season. From the basin, climb a left-angling ramp system to gain Monument Peak's south/southeast ridge at about 6,900 ft, then follow a long talus traverse toward the summit. The final section involves roughly a half-pitch of Class 3 (locally Class 3-4) scrambling where the ridge merges with the southeast slopes, sometimes complicated by a steep snowfield just below the true summit that can still require an ice axe (or a class 3/4 rock detour around its left side) into midsummer. Three alternative approaches exist: dropping in from 6,960-ft Slate Pass on the Harts Pass Road down to the Robinson Creek Trail No. 478 and Ferguson Lake Trail No. 474A (reportedly the easiest, though not shortest, reaching the same basin from the north); via the Buckskin Ridge Trailhead just past Harts Pass on Trail No. 498, crossing the Middle Fork Pasayten River and picking up Robinson Creek Trail No. 478 then Ferguson Lake Trail No. 474A; or a longer approach from the Lost Creek/Monument Creek trailhead side. Whichever line is used, expect long, remote travel with significant off-trail brush and route-finding on the final miles — carry a map/GPS and budget extra time.
row.descent_text: This is a walk-off — there is no rappelling on the standard scramble route. Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the Class 3 (occasionally 3-4) rock/talus off the summit block to regain the south/southeast ridge at roughly 6,900 ft, then descend the left-angling ramp system back into Lower Monument Basin, topping off water at the lake-outlet creek if needed, before climbing back up to the Lake Mountain saddle (~7,400 ft) and dropping to high camp at Lake of the Woods. Where a summit snowfield was crossed on the ascent, most parties recross it on foot (or skirt around its left side on rock) rather than glissade, since it can remain firm or icy well into summer. The main descent hazards are loose talus, exposed Class 3 scrambling near the summit, and route-finding fatigue — several parties describe finishing the final talus slopes back to camp by headlamp. No fixed anchors, bolts, or rappel gear are used on this route. From camp, retrace whichever approach trail was used — Pistol Pass and the Eureka Creek ford back to the Monument Creek Trailhead, or the Ferguson Lake/Robinson Creek trail back to Slate Pass or the Buckskin Ridge Trailhead — to reach the road.

itinerary.cal: Pasayten Wilderness needs only a self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead; the Eureka Creek ford is highest and most hazardous in early summer, so most parties go in August-September once flows drop and the fords are easier.

Most parties start early and still finish near dark.

climate.typical: The Pasayten sits in the rain shadow of the Cascade crest, giving it a drier, more continental climate than the west-side Cascades: big day/night temperature swings, less abundant water than west-side ranges, and a real risk of afternoon thunderstorms in summer.

bySeason.fall: First snow can arrive by late September; a good, less-crowded window often opens in early-to-mid September.
bySeason.spring: Still largely snowbound at this elevation; the Harts Pass road corridor and high trails typically aren't clear until late June.
bySeason.summer: Warm, dry days with cold nights; afternoon thunderstorms are common — plan to be off exposed ridges by early afternoon.
bySeason.winter: Full winter conditions and no vehicle access — the access road is snow-closed.

approach_variants.name: Lower Monument Basin and the left-angling ramp
approach_variants.notes: Monument is the most rugged thing in this group and sits nearly as an island, with Eureka Creek wrapping three sides of it. The travelled approach is the Monument Creek trail from the Lost River road: well maintained through old growth for about four miles to the Eureka Creek confluence, then unmaintained, brushy and deadfall-choked, with a ford of Eureka Creek that can run thigh to waist deep in early summer. From there the abandoned tread climbs onto Pistol Ridge and over Pistol Pass, and most parties camp near Lake of the Woods. Three other approaches exist off Slate Pass and Buckskin Ridge by way of the Ferguson Lake trail and reach the same basin from the north. Summit day is long enough that finishing the last talus by headlamp is common.
hazards: Loose blocky talus on the whole upper mountain
Exposed scrambling on the final summit block
A snowfield below the summit that can hold firm or icy into midsummer
Eureka Creek ford, cold and high with early-season snowmelt
Faint, unmaintained tread beyond Pistol Pass, worse on the return
Long, remote, multi-day approach with no cell service
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base of the climb is marked by water, which is convenient because you should be stopping there anyway. From high camp, traverse northwest to the saddle below Lake Mountain around 7,400 ft, then drop into Lower Monument Basin at roughly 6,100 ft. The outlet creek running from the lake in that basin is the last dependable water on the peak and it sits directly beneath the route; late in the season it can shrink to a trickle but the drainage is still obvious. Fill bottles, then look up and to the left for a ramp system that angles left across the face above you. That ramp is the start of the climbing and it is the feature to identify: it is a continuous weakness slanting up and left, not a gully, and it delivers you onto the south ridge crest at about 6,900 ft. Once you are on the crest the ground flattens into a broad talus highway that runs for well over a mile toward the summit, and that flatness is itself the confirmation that you gained the ridge in the right place rather than on a side rib. Two things mislead near the top. A false summit around 8,000 ft takes a short scramble and looks convincing; the true top is a distinctive leaning horn of granite, so if what you are standing on is not leaning you are not finished. And a steep snowfield sits just below the true summit well into midsummer, which can be crossed with an axe or turned on rock to its left, but should not be glissaded on the way down because it stays firm.

climbing_route.label: Left-angling ramp system to the south/southeast ridge
climbing_route.notes: From Lower Monument Basin (~6,100 ft), climb a left-angling ramp system to gain Monument Peak's south/southeast ridge at about 6,900 ft. The lake-outlet creek in the basin is the last dependable water for the summit push and can shrink to a trickle late in the season.

climbing_route.label: Long talus traverse toward the summit
climbing_route.notes: Follow the ridge on a long talus traverse toward the summit.

climbing_route.label: Final half-pitch where the ridge merges with the southeast slopes
climbing_route.notes: Roughly a half-pitch of Class 3 (locally Class 3-4) scrambling where the ridge merges with the southeast slopes, sometimes complicated by a steep snowfield just below the true summit that can still require an ice axe — or a class 3/4 rock detour around its left side — into midsummer.

bivy.name: Lake of the Woods and the Eureka Falls camp
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Monument Peak and Lake Mountain and it is worth being clear that they are approached from a completely different point on the Harts Pass road than the crest peaks — the Monument Creek trailhead at about 2,400 feet, roughly seven miles up from Mazama, thirteen miles short of the pass. The route runs up the Lost River valley, crosses Eureka Creek where the bridge has been out in the past, then climbs the abandoned Pistol Ridge trail to Pistol Pass at 7,100 feet before dropping to the lake. Expect around thirty miles and thirteen thousand feet over three to four days for both summits — Monument at 8,592 feet by its south ridge, Lake Mountain at 8,371 by its east ridge, each a short steep scramble from the basin. The Pistol Ridge trail is unmaintained and route-finding through it is part of the work. An alternative for parties coming from the north is to drop off Lake Mountain into Eureka Creek and camp near the south fork, which shortens things considerably if the traverse is already underway. Late September brings the larches and cold clear nights; earlier in the summer the long dry climb to the pass is punishing.
bivy.water: The lake is dependable and so is Eureka Creek down in the valley. Between them, though, is the crux: the creek crossing about four miles in is the last certain water before an eight-mile climb gaining five thousand feet to the pass, and in a hot late-summer spell that carry is what makes or breaks the day. Fill completely at the creek.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Monument Creek trailhead kiosk, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, and the usual prohibition on tying animals to trees overnight.
bivy.capacity: Lake of the Woods is a small alpine basin with room for a couple of tents on the benches below Lake Mountain. The Eureka Falls site down in the valley near the confluence of the Lost River and Eureka Creek is a forested camp taking a party or two. Neither is developed.

row.name: Southwest Slopes
row.fa: Joe Firey, Joan Firey, John Meulemans, Irene Meulemans — July 6, 1966 (first ascent of the true/West summit; the East Peak, a lower subsidiary point, had been reached separately in 1940 by Fred Beckey, Jim Crooks, and Ed Kennedy)

crampons (early/mid-season for the Silent Lakes approach couloir)
trekking poles (cross-country travel through Fisher Creek Basin talus and heather)
hazards: extensive loose ('chossy') rock on the summit ridge's gullies and ledges — rockfall onto climbers below is a documented hazard

row.overview: Mount Arriva (8,215 ft) is a long, broken summit ridge at the east end of the Ragged Ridge group in North Cascades National Park, about 1.6 mi southwest of Easy Pass — though it stays hidden from both the pass and SR-20 despite that proximity. The ridge has two high points: East Peak (~8,160+ ft), first climbed by Fred Beckey, Jim Crooks, and Ed Kennedy in August 1940, and the higher true (west) summit, first reached July 6, 1966 by Joe and Joan Firey with John and Irene Meulemans. There is no trail to the peak — parties approach off-trail through Fisher Creek Basin and the Silent Lakes basin, then climb class 3 (occasionally class 4, depending on the exact line) rock on Arriva's south/southwest ridge and ledge systems to the summit. It's commonly combined with nearby Fisher Peak, Kitling Peak, or Graybeard Peak as a multi-day trip.
row.beta: This is a remoteness-and-navigation objective more than a technical one — the documented 'easiest route' is class 3 (YDS) scrambling with no reported roped climbing, but it sits far off any maintained trail. No other named technical route (rock face, ridge, or couloir line) is documented on this peak; the subsidiary East Peak (8,160+ ft) was reached separately in 1940 by Fred Beckey's party, likely by a similar approach but not confirmed as the same exact line.
row.turnaround: Given the multi-hour, mostly off-trail approach and return, set a firm turnaround time based on remaining daylight and weather rather than distance to the summit — deteriorating weather or a late start on this exposed, trail-less shoulder can easily turn a long day into a benighted one.
row.rock_grade: Class 3 (YDS) — scramble, no roped climbing on the standard line
row.permit: No climbing permit. Every overnight stay inside North Cascades National Park requires a backcountry permit - $10 per person plus a $6 reservation fee - and permits are limited. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is needed to park at developed trailheads.
row.comms: Deep, seldom-visited North Cascades National Park backcountry, more than 5 miles from the highway with no maintained trail for the final approach; expect no reliable cell coverage and carry a satellite communicator/PLB.
row.descent: Reverse the ascent line down the south/southwest ridge and gully/ledge system back to the ~7,800-ft notch and 7,200-ft saddle above Silent Lakes. The rock is loose in places — one trip report documents a 'surfboard-size' rock dislodged by a descending climber that narrowly missed party members below, so descend one at a time and stay out of the fall line. If descending via the Silent Lakes headwall couloir, expect firm snow/ice early season and a loose rock gully late season; many parties prefer the broken heather/cliff ramps just left of the couloir instead.
obj_haz: Long, complex, mostly off-trail approach through Fisher Basin with real route-finding difficulty
Lingering snowfields on the Easy Pass Trail into early summer; NPS advises carrying an ice axe
Loose, exfoliating tonalite typical of North Cascades scramble terrain
Very remote — no cell coverage, hours from help; small mistakes carry outsized consequences
Glaciated neighboring peaks (Katsuk, Mesahchie) indicate genuinely alpine, weather-exposed terrain

pro_tips: If short on time, camp at the head of Fisher Creek Basin (~6,000 ft) below the Silent Lakes headwall — Arriva can reasonably be climbed round trip from there in a long day.
Favor the broken heather/cliff ramps left of the Silent Lakes couloir once it melts out late-season; the couloir itself turns into a loose rock gully.
Descend the summit gullies one at a time — loose rock dislodged by climbers above has narrowly missed parties below on this route.
watch_out: The Silent Lakes headwall couloir/gully is the technical crux of the trip, not the class 3 summit scrambling.
The boot path beyond the Fisher Camp junction disappears at avalanche debris — expect sustained cross-country travel and routefinding from there to Silent Lakes.
Cell coverage is unreliable to nonexistent in Fisher Creek Basin and at Silent Lakes.
row.pro_needs: Generally an unroped class 3 scramble; rope optional for the exposed summit area.
row.best_season: Late July through September for the most reliable snow-free travel; ice axe (and often crampons) are still useful into July on the Silent Lakes approach couloir and the north side of Easy Pass. SR-20 access is closed entirely in winter.
row.approach: There is no trail to Mount Arriva itself; the standard approach is a 2-3 day off-trail trip via Fisher Creek Basin and Silent Lakes. From the Easy Pass Trailhead (3,700 ft, SR-20 between mileposts 151 and 152), hike the Easy Pass Trail 3.5-3.6 mi and about 2,800 ft to Easy Pass (~6,500 ft), then descend the west side into Fisher Creek Basin. Near the Fisher Camp junction, a boot path heads east/up-valley but fades after about ten minutes at a pile of avalanche-downed trees; from there travel is cross-country up through meadows to the head of Fisher Creek (~6,000 ft — Fisher Overlook Camp is a good base if short on time). From the head of the valley, climb the roughly 1,000-ft headwall to Silent Lakes (~7,000 ft) via either the obvious snow/ice couloir (steeper than it looks, and melts into a loose rock gully by late season) or the broken heather/cliff ramps to its left; ice axe and crampons are useful here into mid-summer. From a camp at Upper Silent Lake, a roughly 1-mile westerly traverse across heather leads to a 7,200-ft saddle, then a rising traverse across a talus bowl gains a key 7,800-ft notch on Arriva's south ridge for the final scramble to the summit.

itinerary.cal: North Cascades NP requires a backcountry permit for camping at Fisher Overlook/Silent Lakes year-round; about 60% of sites are reservable in advance on recreation.gov, the rest are walk-up, and reserved trips request their permit by email no more than three days before the start date.

days.note: Hike the Easy Pass Trail to the pass (~2.3 hr, +2,800 ft), then drop about 1,300 ft into Fisher Creek Basin where the trail fades into cross-country travel through meadows past a big waterfall. Continue up the obvious gully to camp at Upper Silent Lake, with views across to Black Peak.

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day, roughly 14-16 mile round trip: about 5,600 ft of cumulative approach gain to a Silent Lakes camp at 7,000 ft, a short ~5 hr summit day on Arriva's south ridge (1,900 ft round trip), and a full day to hike back out; strong parties sometimes compress the summit push and exit into one long day, or extend the trip to also tag Fisher Peak.

access.fees: Trailhead parking requires a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency (America the Beautiful) Pass, or Recreation.gov Digital Day Pass ($5/vehicle/day or $30/year). Overnight backcountry permits — effectively required for this multi-day objective — cost $10/person plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee.
access.notes: The trailhead and the trail up to Easy Pass are Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District); everything beyond the pass, including Fisher Creek Basin, Silent Lakes and the peak, is inside North Cascades National Park. No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: No dogs beyond the national park boundary, including at Easy Pass. No pack animals at the trailhead. Stay on durable surfaces — alpine vegetation in the meadows is fragile.
access.permit: A wilderness/backcountry permit is required for all overnight stays; reserve a site on recreation.gov, then request the permit itself by email no more than three days before the start date; walk-up permits are issued in person at a park permit station the day before or the day of the trip. Camping is prohibited at Easy Pass itself and in the pass meadows — designated camps on the Fisher Creek Trail are Fisher Camp, Cosho Camp, and Junction Camp; Fisher Creek Basin/Silent Lakes camping is cross-country zone camping (ask the WIC about current quotas).
access.closures: SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes for winter, typically early December through April or May depending on snowpack, cutting off all access to the Easy Pass Trailhead; check WSDOT mountain pass reports before planning a trip.
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness); the Easy Pass Trailhead itself sits on Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District, just outside the park boundary.
access.land_manager: North Cascades National Park (trailhead on Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at the Easy Pass trailhead on SR-20 between mileposts 151 and 152, which has a self-issue station — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass / Interagency Pass for trailhead parking, plus an NPS wilderness/backcountry permit for the overnight approach.

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades NP wilderness permit — quota, fee
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov; permits for Cascade River Road trailheads must be picked up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.

road.name: North Cascades Highway (SR-20)
road.driveNote: Easy Pass Trailhead is on the south side of SR-20 between mileposts 151 and 152 — about 46 mi east of Marblemount or 40 mi west of Winthrop.
road.seasonalGate: Typically closes early December through April/May at gates near Ross Dam (MP134) and Silver Star (MP171), sometimes shifting to Newhalem (MP120)/Early Winters (MP178) later in the season; check WSDOT before planning.

climate.typical: Marine west coast climate with heavy orographic precipitation off Pacific fronts. Winters bring deep, wet snowpack that closes SR-20 and buries the approach into early summer; summers (roughly August-September) offer the most reliable snow-free travel, though afternoon thunderstorms are common on this exposed ridge.

emergency.notes: Cell service is unreliable to nonexistent in Fisher Creek Basin and at Silent Lakes; a satellite messenger is recommended given the multi-day, off-trail nature of the approach.
emergency.county: The summit sits on the Skagit/Chelan county line; the Easy Pass Trailhead and the entire approach through Fisher Creek Basin and Silent Lakes lie within Skagit County.
emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades National Park Wilderness Information Center, Marblemount — (360) 854-7245
emergency.nearestHospital: This is a remote, multi-day objective with no nearby hospital. Serious trauma is typically evacuated by NPS or military helicopter to Harborview Medical Center in Seattle; by road, the closest hospitals are roughly 60 mi east via Winthrop (Three Rivers Hospital, Brewster) or 70+ mi west via Marblemount (United General District Hospital, Sedro-Woolley, and Skagit Valley Hospital, Mount Vernon).
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911 (NPS coordinates search and rescue within the park, typically with Skagit County Sheriff and county SAR assisting)

crowds.peakTraffic: Light even in peak window (mid-July-September); Easy Pass trail itself sees hikers/scramblers, but the cross-country push to Arriva's SW Slopes sees only a small fraction of that traffic
crowds.estimatePerSeason: unknown - low-traffic; only isolated documented trip reports found (e.g., a single 2019 combined Arriva/Fisher Peak report), suggesting well under 20 parties per season

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strenuous full day: Easy Pass trail approach followed by significant off-trail basin travel and elevation gain before the scramble even starts; plan for a long, sustained effort
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Most parties carry a full overnight pack to camp at Silent Lakes; a light day pack (roughly 15-25 lbs) suits only fast parties doing the whole trip car-to-car in one very long day

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long: Easy Pass trail plus substantial cross-country basin travel to reach the base of the SW Slopes; realistically a full-day approach-and-climb effort, usually broken with a camp at Silent Lakes or in the upper basin; fast parties do it car-to-car in one very long day
requiredSkills: Off-trail/cross-country route-finding
Exposed Class 3 scrambling on loose rock
Early-season steep snow travel and self-arrest (approach basin)
Backcountry navigation (map/compass/GPS) away from trail
Sound judgment on afternoon-storm bailout timing
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate-to-advanced scrambler comfortable with sustained Class 3 terrain and off-trail/cross-country route-finding without a maintained path to the summit

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September, with August generally the most reliable stretch

July.reason: Existing best-season starts mid-July; approach snow can still linger into July, so early July is less reliable than late July

June.reason: Approach basin still snow-covered; per existing climate/hazards data this means steep, avalanche-prone snow low on the route and early-season conditions best suited to parties with snow-travel skills

August.reason: Prime scrambling window; most consistent rock and driest approach conditions

September.reason: Stable but shorter days in fall, with early storms possible; still a solid window but with more weather risk toward month's end

weather.typical: Alpine North Cascades weather with rapid changes possible
weather.probability: Afternoon storms are a hazard here; treat convective build-up as a common summer pattern requiring an early start and summit-by-noon timing

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Sustained Class 3 exposure on loose rock on the upper slopes; a fall or dislodged rock has real consequence, and a slip on the steep early-season snow in the approach basin could result in a long, injurious slide

avalanche.zone: No NWAC zone maps precisely onto this peak; the nearest analog corridor is the North Cascades Highway/East Slopes North region, but this route is climbed as a dry-season scramble outside NWAC's active winter forecasting period, so no formal seasonal avalanche forecast applies

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel on the SW Slopes scramble route itself (a small glacier exists on the peak's northeast side per outside sources, but it is not part of this route)

gaps: No verified single round-trip mileage/elevation-gain figure for Arriva alone — trip reports combine it with Fisher Peak/Silent Lakes side objectives, so the on-file dist_km/gain_ft are estimates derived from waypoint geometry, not measured GPS data.
The exact difficulty of the summit gully/ledge system (solid class 3 vs. short class 4 moves) varies by which line/notch a party takes and isn't fully standardized across sources.

approach_variants.name: Easy Pass, Fisher Creek Basin and Silent Lakes
approach_variants.notes: There is no trail to this peak. From the Easy Pass Trailhead on SR-20 the maintained trail climbs to Easy Pass, and from there you descend the west side into Fisher Creek Basin. Near the Fisher Camp junction a boot path heads up-valley but fades within about ten minutes at a pile of avalanche-downed trees; from there travel is cross-country up through meadows to the head of Fisher Creek, where an overlook camp works well as a base if you are short of time. From the head of the valley the headwall to Silent Lakes goes either by the obvious snow and ice couloir — steeper than it looks from below, and degrading into a loose rock gully by late season — or by the broken heather and cliff ramps to its left. An axe, and often crampons, are useful here into midsummer. From a camp at Upper Silent Lake, a roughly westerly traverse across heather leads to a saddle around 7,200 ft, then a rising traverse across a talus bowl gains the notch on the peak's south ridge where the scrambling starts.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September for the most reliable snow-free travel. An axe and often crampons are still worth carrying into July for the headwall couloir and the north side of Easy Pass. The highway itself is shut in winter.
hazards: extensive loose rock in the summit ridge's gullies and ledges, with rockfall onto anyone below
steep snow and ice in the headwall couloir to Silent Lakes — the real technical crux of the trip, not the summit scrambling
long off-trail route-finding through Fisher Creek Basin with no tread beyond the Fisher Camp junction
avalanche paths on the flanks near Easy Pass in early season
black bears through Fisher Creek Basin and the Easy Pass meadows
afternoon thunderstorms on an exposed ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding: AN ERODED BLACK DIKE SPLITS THE SUMMIT BLOCK, AND THAT SLOT IS THE ROUTE. The rising traverse across the talus bowl tops out at a pronounced notch in the south ridge at roughly 7,600 to 7,800 ft; from the notch, scramble up good rock along the crest until the summit block itself blocks the way. Look for a narrow defile cut into the block — a dark band that has weathered back into a slot, so the feature reads as a black stripe with a groove eroded along it. Climb the defile until you can traverse leftward on a sloping ramp that puts you back on the south ridge crest, then scramble the crest to the top. If the block above you is uniform pale rock with no dark band running through it, you are not at the defile: traverse and keep looking rather than forcing the face, because the ledges here are chossy and everything you dislodge falls on the party below. A second check: the correct line never asks for a rope. If you find yourself committed to moves you would want protected, you have gone up the face rather than through the slot.

climbing_route.label: South ridge from the 7,800-ft notch
climbing_route.notes: A rising traverse across a talus bowl gains a key 7,800-ft notch on Arriva's south ridge; from the notch a final scramble leads to the summit. The source text describes nothing further about this ground.

bivy.notes: Alpine lakes between Mount Arriva and Fisher Peak, reached off-trail from upper Fisher Creek basin below Easy Pass. The upper lake sits near 7,000 ft and is the usual base for Arriva's south side.

bivy.name: Easy Pass trailhead, SR 20
bivy.notes: This is the only practical trailhead for Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah and Mount Arriva, and it is worth understanding what the walk in costs before committing to it. The trail climbs roughly three thousand feet in a little under four miles, gently through forest at first and then in steep switchbacks up a headwall of loose rock with real exposure to weather; the name is old optimism and nothing about it is easy under a climbing pack. Snow holds on the upper switchbacks and in the basin above into July in an ordinary year and later after a heavy winter, and that traverse is where parties turn around. There is a toilet at the lot and parties routinely sleep in the car here before a pre-dawn start. Dogs may come only as far as the pass, because the top of the pass is the national park boundary.
bivy.water: None at the lot. Granite Creek is crossed on a bridge a few minutes up the trail and is the last easy water low on the approach.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit is needed on the forest side of the pass. THE MOMENT YOU CROSS THE PASS THE RULES CHANGE COMPLETELY — see the Ragged Ridge and Fisher Creek entries below.
bivy.capacity: A small lot with room for roughly ten cars, on a short spur off the highway between mileposts 151 and 152. It is genuinely small and can be full on a good weekend.

name: South Route
prior_findings: Camp card says Crescent Creek Basin is north of the crest (it is south). ALSO: grade/FA/face/beta are the 2003 east arete (II 5.10a); overview/itinerary/pro tips describe a 5.7 line from the Eye Col. Decide which climb the row is.

earlier_research.evidence: Two different lines are merged in this row. The 2003 AAJ account lists East Twin Needle (II 5.10a) as one of three first ascents on the east-to-west Southern Pickets traverse and describes the 'tremendously exposed east arête' — that is where the grade, rock_grade, fa, face and beta come from. Only one source grades the Eye Col line (5.7), so the row's grade/fa/face/beta cannot yet be rewritten to it with two agreeing sources; which line this row is (name 'South Route' vs the 5.10a data) is an owner decision. So approach_variants[0].baseFinding is right and climbing_route[1]/the approach's final clause are wrong — but the correct replacement text (the Eye Col line's own description) depends on the unresolved identity question above, so no patch is written.

The 2003 party (Wallace, Haley, Bunker, July 27, 2003) is credited with East Twin Needle's II 5.10a east arête. No source names a first-ascent party for the Eye Col line; the 1932 Degenhardt party is credited with 'Twin Needles' generally (the higher West Twin). Depends on the identity decision; no patch.

The 2022 AAJ note descended these same south-facing gullies with repeated rappels, and the 2009 report records a chockstone rappel — not plain 4th-class ground. So the waypoint note, baseFinding and variant notes are consistent (each describes a different stretch); only the itinerary's '4th-class scrambling' understates it.

The move to the lower 6,050 ft camp is kept as an option.

row.overview: East Twin Needle (7,868 ft) is the eastern and slightly lower of the Twin Needles pinnacles in the Southern Pickets, 0.55 mi west of Mount Terror and just east of its taller sister summit, West Twin Needle (7,936 ft). Both needles were first climbed together on August 17, 1932 by William Degenhardt, James Martin, and Herb Strandberg. Composed of solid Skagit gneiss, the pair rises above Crescent Creek Basin near the Mustard Glacier and is almost always climbed as a linked outing from one camp given the shared, multi-day approach. Besides the moderate line described here, East Twin Needle also has a notably harder, more direct East Arête (rated II 5.10a, climbed during the 2003 Southern Picket Range enchainment) and a 2022-established North Buttress ("Thread of Gneiss," 2,000 ft, 5.9, 9 pitches) - be sure you're on the intended, moderate line.
row.beta: Established on July 27, 2003 by Mark Bunker, Colin Haley, and Wayne Wallace during their four-day, 14-summit Complete Southern Pickets Traverse (rated overall VI 5.10+, ~50 technical pitches), this was one of only three genuine first ascents on that trip (with The Rake and Himmelhorn). Wallace described the climbing as requiring some traversing around the ridgecrest and 'still very difficult ascending the tremendously exposed east arête.' It is graded II 5.10a. Because it was climbed mid-enchainment rather than as a stand-alone objective, no independent topo or pitch-by-pitch account has been published; parties repeating it do so almost exclusively as part of a Southern Pickets traverse rather than as a dedicated route.
row.turnaround: At least 2-3 hours of daylight remaining for descent; turn around by early afternoon given the complex descent and potential for afternoon weather deterioration in the Pickets.
row.rappels: Multiple rappels on descent (two 60-meter ropes recommended)
row.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (walk-up only, issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; the Southern Picket cross-country zones cannot be reserved in advance).
row.comms: The Picket Range is a remote wilderness area with no reliable cell phone coverage. Satellite messaging devices (garmin inReach, Zoleo, or smartphones with satellite features) are essential for emergency communication. Reception for satellite devices may be limited by steep terrain and narrow gullies.
row.descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock and snow bridge hazards. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.

Extremely remote setting with limited retreat options

row.detailed_rack: Recommended rack includes a single set of BD Camalots from .3 to #2 (gneiss climbing favors cams due to parallel crack systems), a selection of passive protection (wedges/nuts), approximately 10-15 quickdraws, slings, cordelette, and two full-length 60-meter dynamic ropes. Given the gneiss rock type and mixed terrain, emphasis should be placed on camming devices that can handle variable crack widths.

row.pro_needs: The South Route requires solid rock climbing skills at 5.7 grade with competence in multi-pitch trad climbing. Leaders should be experienced at route-finding on complex alpine faces and comfortable with modest class 4 scrambling. Ability to place protection quickly and accurately in shifting rock and gneiss terrain is essential. This is an alpine expedition-style climb requiring self-rescue competence and remote wilderness mountaineering experience.
row.approach: Start at the Goodell Creek Cross-Country Zone Access Trailhead off SR-20 near milepost 119 (elev. ~600'). Follow the Goodell Creek Trail, an old forestry roadbed running through open forest along Goodell Creek, for roughly 4-4.5 miles. Near the trail's end, leave the maintained tread at a large cairn marking the start of the unmaintained Terror Basin/Barrier climbers' path and ford Terror Creek (can run high with snowmelt in early/mid summer - scout for a safe crossing). From the creek, the route shoots straight up the increasingly brushy crest of 'The Barrier,' a steep, dry ridge with essentially no water until small snowmelt puddles appear around 5,400'. Timberline is reached near 5,600', where travel opens onto slabs and heather in 'Stump Hollow' between the Barrier crest and the Chopping Block. Most parties camp on the Chopping Block ridge (~6,400'), making the car-to-camp day roughly 6-7.5 miles with about 5,800-6,000' of gain - a full, strenuous day, and the crux of the whole trip for many parties (loose talus, fading cairns/flagging, and route-finding through brush make The Barrier notorious for turning parties around). Parties wanting a camp nearer the Needles can instead drop about 200-250' off the ridge crest into Crescent Creek Basin and traverse roughly a mile cross-country (talus, slabs, occasional snow) staying near 5,800', to a camp below Mount Terror at about 6,050' near two streams fed by overhead slabs (reliable water, unlike the Barrier). From this basin camp, descend about 300' below the moraine to the head of Crescent Creek, then work up and around buttresses toward the braided, loose south-facing gullies beneath the Eye Col, the notch separating East and West Twin Needle. The final few hundred feet to the col and onto the route involve steep, loose gully climbing with real route-finding uncertainty (this south side has comparatively sparse route information and can feel disorienting in cloud or low light) before gaining the exposed southeast ridge/east arête that the route follows to the summit.
row.descent_text: Most parties reverse the route: downclimb the south-facing gullies back to the Eye Col and continue down into Crescent Creek Basin, a mix of class 4 downclimbing and short rappels off natural anchors (rock horns and slings - no bolted stations reported) on loose rock; expect 1-3 short single-rope rappels depending on snow coverage and the exact gully taken. East Twin Needle is frequently climbed in combination with West Twin Needle as part of a Southern Pickets enchainment; in that case parties continue the ridge west and exit via the Himmelhorn-West Twin Needle notch rather than re-descending the Eye Col gullies. That exit is better documented: two rappels using double 60m ropes are needed below the notch to get past vertical slabs, landing on grass and sloping rock around 6,800'; from there the route continues down a south gully with additional short rappels over vertical rock above a lingering snowfield before regaining Crescent Creek Basin. All anchors encountered on this descent are natural (horns, chockstones, slings) - carry cord/webbing for anchor building and expect to leave gear. From Crescent Creek Basin, reverse the approach: back up and over the Chopping Block ridge, down The Barrier (roughly 4,300' of descent to Terror Creek - loose and brushy, arguably harder in descent than ascent), across Terror Creek, and out the Goodell Creek Trail to the trailhead.
row.bail: Reverse the approach over the Barrier back to Terror Creek and Goodell Creek. There is no quick bail once committed above the Eye Col - retreat means downclimbing/rappelling the same gully system you climbed.

itinerary.cal: North Cascades NP requires a backcountry permit for Terror/Crescent Creek Basin camps, and the Barrier is normally only safely crossable July-September once seasonal snow bridges and the approach brush have opened up.

days.note: A grueling cross-country day: old roadbed and steep, brushy boot path from Goodell Creek Trailhead past Terror Creek, then a loose, exposed scramble across the Barrier into the Crescent Creek Basin drainage. Most parties camp on a flat bench or col around 6,000-6,400 ft, close under the Chopping Block/Twin Needles group.
